title: GMO Internet — the $50 million ransom Japan refused

scenes.narration: [serious] Hackers asked a Japanese company for 50 million dollars. It said no.
GMO Internet rents cloud desktops, online computers, to currency traders.
On October 20, GMO found a rogue program on customer servers.
Then came an email demanding eight billion yen, about 50 million dollars.
GMO refused. It told customers to back up and unplug their PCs.
The attackers posted stolen data anyway. Some traders saw trades they never made.
Then GMO struck back with a bounty of up to one million dollars.
No one is named yet. They wanted 50 million. Now there's a million-dollar bounty on them.

facts.claim: GMO's Onamae.com Desktop Cloud hosts Windows desktops used for FX trading
On October 20, 2026, GMO confirmed a third party had installed an unauthorized program on some customers' server environments
GMO counts up to 26,739 servers as potentially affected (not a confirmed count of break-ins)
The hackers emailed GMO demanding about 8 billion yen (about $50 million); per CEO Masatoshi Kumagai's blog the demand was in cryptocurrency; received Oct 21
GMO said it would not pay because it could not guarantee deletion of data; urged users to back up and disconnect before the noon deadline
Customers were told on Oct 27 to back up data, then disconnect, shut down and unplug PCs before noon
GMO said it believes the attacker published information linked to its customers and business (Oct 27)
OANDA Japan confirmed a third party traded on some customer accounts using credentials believed to have come from GMO's servers
On Oct 28 GMO launched the GMO Cybercrime Bounty, up to $1 million for tips leading to an arrest or international wanted notice; GMO has not named a group or said how attackers got in
